title: How can I call you in? (1.2–1.5)
word: How can I call you in?
hook: Augustine asks how the God who fills everything can come into him
tomorrow: can a baby who can't talk yet already be jealous?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the first page of the Confessions: made for God, and our heart is restless until it rests in him. The restlessness had a direction.

The doorbell rings, and the living room looks like a laundry basket exploded: cleats by the couch, mail on every chair, last night's pots still in the sink. Whoever's out there, the first reflex is the same. Wait. Don't come in yet. Augustine has that reflex, only bigger. In the pages after his famous first line, he wants to call on God, and then he stops. To call on God, he notices, is to call him in. And the one at the door already fills heaven and earth. So where, in one small, messy person, is there room?
screen: `THE DOORBELL, AND THE MESS.` → `TO CALL ON IS TO CALL IN.` → `WHERE IS THERE ROOM?`

segments.voice: His questions tumble out. Heaven and earth are filled with God; do they hold him? If God fills everything, what's left over once they're full? Is there a part of him here and a bigger part there? Augustine doesn't solve it with a diagram. He lets the questions stand, then turns them around. I could not be at all, he says, unless God were in me. Or rather, unless I were in him. The problem was never that God is far away. A few pages on, the puzzle becomes a plea, and the house becomes his soul. In Pusey's translation: "Narrow is the mansion of my soul; enlarge Thou it, that Thou mayest enter in. It is ruinous; repair Thou it." He admits there's something in it that would offend God's eyes, and asks who will clean it, if not God. Look at the order. Not a better house first and an invitation later. He asks God to do the enlarging and the repairing himself, after he's inside. Here's the part to tell a friend tonight. Catholics say something close at every Mass, just before Communion, borrowing a Roman centurion's words from the Gospel: Lord, I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof; only say the word. Same small house. Same knock.
screen: `DO HEAVEN AND EARTH HOLD GOD?` · `I COULD NOT BE, UNLESS I WERE IN HIM.` · `ENLARGE IT. REPAIR IT.` · `THE CENTURION'S ROOF, AT EVERY MASS.` · then, large: `COME IN.`

segments.voice: Rest your hands open on your knees, palms up, like a door left unlatched. Don't tidy anything first; let your mind be as cluttered as it really is. If you pray, you can borrow Augustine's plain words, enlarge it, repair it; if not, just keep the hands open and stop straightening up for a while.
How can I call you in? Augustine's question in book one: how the God who fills everything could come into one small, ruined room.
screen: `HOW CAN I CALL YOU IN? — today's word`.

segments.voice: Pocket this one: come in, and let the repairs happen from the inside, not out on the porch. See you tomorrow.
